Apple___Apple_scab.description: Apple scab is caused by the fungus Venturia inaequalis. It produces dark, olive-green to black lesions on leaves, fruit, and sometimes twigs. Severe infections cause premature leaf drop and unmarketable fruit.

methods.name: Neem Oil Spray
methods.instructions: Mix 5 ml neem oil with 1 litre of water and a few drops of liquid soap as emulsifier. Spray thoroughly on all leaf surfaces.

methods.name: Sulfur-Based Fungicide
methods.instructions: Apply wettable sulfur at 3 g per litre of water. Do not apply when temperature exceeds 30°C.

methods.name: Bordeaux Mixture
methods.instructions: Prepare a 1% Bordeaux mixture (10 g copper sulfate + 10 g lime per litre). Spray before bud break and again at petal fall.

chemical_treatment.warning: Do not apply within 14 days of harvest. Rotate fungicide classes to prevent resistance.

prevention: Remove and destroy fallen infected leaves in autumn
Prune trees to improve air circulation within the canopy
Plant scab-resistant apple varieties when possible
Avoid overhead irrigation to keep foliage dry
Apply dormant-season copper spray before bud break
spread_checklist: Rake and remove all fallen leaves around infected trees
Prune out heavily scabbed twigs and branches
Disinfect pruning tools with 70% isopropyl alcohol between cuts
Avoid working with trees when foliage is wet
Apply protective fungicide to nearby healthy trees
Monitor adjacent trees daily for 2 weeks for new lesions
Bag and dispose of infected fruit - do not compost

actions: Remove all visibly infected leaves and fruit from the tree
Apply emergency fungicide spray (captan or mancozeb)
Begin scheduled fungicide spray program
Improve air circulation by selective pruning
Clean up all fallen debris around the tree base
Continue fungicide applications on schedule
Monitor weather - increase spray frequency during rain
Apply foliar fertilizer to strengthen tree immunity
Plan for resistant variety grafting or replacement
Apply urea spray to fallen leaves to speed decomposition
Schedule dormant copper spray for next spring

Apple___Black_rot.description: Black rot is caused by the fungus Botryosphaeria obtusa. It produces brown, circular lesions with concentric rings ('frogeye' spots) on leaves, and causes dark, rotting cankers on fruit and branches.

methods.name: Copper Fungicide Spray
methods.instructions: Apply copper hydroxide at 2 g per litre of water. Spray at bud break and repeat at petal fall.

methods.name: Neem Oil
methods.instructions: Mix 5 ml neem oil per litre of water with a surfactant. Spray on all foliage and fruit surfaces.

chemical_treatment.warning: Do not apply captan within 14 days of harvest. Avoid mixing captan with oil-based sprays.

prevention: Remove mummified fruit from trees and ground promptly
Prune out dead wood and cankers during dormant season
Maintain proper tree spacing for air circulation
Remove wild or abandoned apple trees nearby that harbor disease
Apply dormant-season fungicide before bud break
spread_checklist: Remove and destroy all mummified and rotting fruit immediately
Prune cankers at least 15 cm below visible infection margin
Disinfect all pruning tools between cuts
Apply wound sealant to large pruning cuts
Bag and dispose of all infected material - do not compost
Spray surrounding healthy trees with protective fungicide
Monitor weekly for new lesion development

actions: Remove all visibly infected fruit and leaves
Prune out any visible cankers on branches
Apply captan or copper fungicide spray
Clean up all fallen debris from around tree base
Continue fungicide spray schedule
Monitor for new frogeye leaf spots or fruit rot
Ensure good sanitation practices in orchard
Remove all remaining mummies and dead wood in winter
Plan dormant-season copper spray
Consider resistant varieties for new plantings

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.description: Cedar apple rust is caused by the fungus Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae. It requires both apple and cedar/juniper trees to complete its life cycle. It produces bright orange-yellow spots on apple leaves and fruit.

methods.name: Sulfur Spray
methods.instructions: Apply wettable sulfur at 3 g per litre of water starting at pink bud stage.

methods.name: Neem Oil
methods.instructions: Mix 5 ml per litre of water. Apply as a preventive during early spring.

pesticides.name: Myclobutanil
pesticides.frequency: Every 14 days from pink bud to 2 weeks after petal fall

chemical_treatment.warning: Most effective when applied preventively. Fungicides do not cure existing infections.

prevention: Remove cedar and juniper trees within 100 metres of apple orchard if possible
Remove galls from cedar trees during winter before they produce spores
Plant rust-resistant apple varieties
Begin fungicide program early (at green tip to pink bud stage)
Improve air circulation through proper pruning
spread_checklist: Remove heavily infected leaves from apple trees
Scout for and remove cedar galls from nearby juniper/cedar trees
Apply protective fungicide to remaining healthy foliage
Monitor weather - spores spread during warm, wet spring weather
Inspect nearby apple trees for early yellow-orange spots
Avoid overhead watering during spore release period

actions: Remove severely infected leaves to reduce inoculum
Apply systemic fungicide (myclobutanil) immediately
Scout for and remove cedar galls from nearby trees
Continue protective fungicide applications
Maintain fungicide schedule through wet weather periods
Monitor for new leaf infections weekly
Plan removal of cedar/juniper trees near orchard
Select resistant apple varieties for future planting
Map rust incidence for next season's management plan

Apple___healthy.description: Your apple leaf appears healthy with no visible signs of disease. The leaf shows normal coloration and structure consistent with a vigorous apple tree.
care_tips: Continue regular watering - deep water weekly during dry periods
Apply balanced fertilizer (10-10-10) in early spring before bud break

Blueberry___healthy.description: Your blueberry leaf looks healthy with no signs of disease or nutrient deficiency. The deep green color indicates good plant vigor.

Apply acidifying fertilizer (ammonium sulfate) in early spring
Mulch heavily with pine needles or wood chips (10-15 cm depth)

Net plants to protect fruit from birds during ripening

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew on cherry is caused by the fungus Podosphaera clandestina. It produces white, powdery fungal growth on leaves, shoots, and sometimes fruit, causing leaf curling and stunted growth.

methods.name: Potassium Bicarbonate Spray
methods.instructions: Dissolve 3 g potassium bicarbonate per litre of water. Add a few drops of liquid soap. Spray all leaf surfaces.

methods.name: Sulfur Spray
methods.instructions: Apply wettable sulfur at 3 g per litre of water. Avoid application above 30°C.

methods.name: Milk Spray
methods.instructions: Mix 1 part whole milk with 9 parts water. The proteins in milk combat the fungus.

chemical_treatment.warning: Alternate between different fungicide classes to prevent resistance. Do not apply within 7 days of harvest.

Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization which promotes succulent growth
Water at the base of trees - avoid wetting foliage
Remove and destroy heavily infected shoots in early spring

Apply fungicide to all trees in the area, not just the infected one
Reduce nitrogen fertilizer applications to slow succulent growth
Improve air circulation by thinning interior branches

Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.description: Your cherry leaf appears healthy with good color and no visible disease symptoms. The tree seems to be in good condition.

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.description: Gray leaf spot is caused by the fungus Cercospora zeae-maydis. It produces rectangular, grayish-tan lesions that follow leaf veins. Severe infections can cause significant yield loss due to premature leaf death.

methods.name: Crop Residue Management
methods.instructions: Till or incorporate corn residue after harvest to reduce overwintering fungal inoculum. This is the most effective organic control.

methods.name: Trichoderma-based Biocontrol
methods.instructions: Apply Trichoderma viride at 5 g per litre of water as a foliar spray.
methods.frequency: Every 14 days starting at V6 growth stage

pesticides.name: Azoxystrobin

pesticides.name: Propiconazole

Plant resistant or tolerant corn hybrids
Till corn residue to reduce inoculum carryover
Avoid planting corn-on-corn in fields with history of gray leaf spot
Ensure proper plant spacing to reduce humidity in the canopy
spread_checklist: Scout remaining corn fields for early symptoms

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.description: Common rust is caused by the fungus Puccinia sorghi. It produces small, circular to elongate, reddish-brown pustules on both leaf surfaces. Severe infections can reduce photosynthesis and grain fill.

methods.name: Resistant Hybrid Selection
methods.instructions: The most effective organic strategy is planting rust-resistant corn hybrids. Consult your seed supplier for resistant options.

methods.name: Neem Oil Spray
methods.instructions: Apply 5 ml neem oil per litre of water with a surfactant.
methods.frequency: Every 7-10 days at first sign of pustules

chemical_treatment.warning: Fungicide application is economically justified only in severe cases or high-value seed corn production.

prevention: Plant resistant corn hybrids - this is the primary defense
Plant early to avoid peak rust spore season
Scout fields regularly starting at V8 stage
Maintain balanced fertility - excess nitrogen increases susceptibility

spread_checklist: Scout all corn fields in the area for early rust pustules

actions: Confirm diagnosis by examining pustule color and distribution

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: Northern leaf blight is caused by the fungus Exserohilum turcicum. It produces large, cigar-shaped, grayish-green lesions (3-15 cm long) on corn leaves. Severe infections can reduce yield by 30-50%.

methods.name: Trichoderma Application

Grape___Black_rot.description: Black rot is caused by the fungus Guignardia bidwellii. It produces circular, tan lesions with dark borders on leaves, and causes fruit to shrivel into hard, black mummies. It is one of the most serious grape diseases.

methods.instructions: Apply copper hydroxide at 2 g per litre of water. Start at bud break.

methods.name: Sulfur Spray

pesticides.name: Myclobutanil

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).description: Huanglongbing (HLB), also known as citrus greening, is caused by the bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus, transmitted by the Asian citrus psyllid. methods.name: Nutritional Therapy

methods.name: Thermotherapy

Squash___Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew on squash is caused by the fungi Podosphaera xanthii and Erysiphe cichoracearum. It produces white, powdery fungal growth on upper leaf surfaces, eventually covering entire leaves and causing them to yellow and die.

methods.name: Milk Spray
methods.instructions: Mix 1 part whole milk to 9 parts water. The proteins have antifungal properties.

methods.name: Neem Oil
methods.instructions: Apply 5 ml neem oil per litre of water with surfactant.

methods.name: Sulfur Spray
methods.instructions: Apply wettable sulfur at 3 g per litre. Do not use above 30°C or within 2 weeks of oil sprays.

chemical_treatment.warning: Powdery mildew develops resistance quickly. Always rotate between different fungicide classes.

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot on tomato is caused by several Xanthomonas species. It produces small, dark, water-soaked spots on leaves, stems, and fruit. Leaf spots may have yellow halos and can cause severe defoliation.

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.description: Two-spotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae) are tiny arachnid pests, not a disease. They feed on leaf undersides, causing stippling (tiny yellow dots), bronzing, and eventually leaf death. Fine webbing is visible in severe infestations.

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV) is transmitted by whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci). methods.instructions: Apply 5 ml neem oil per litre of water. Targets whiteflies and disrupts their feeding.

methods.name: Reflective Mulch
methods.instructions: Use silver or aluminium reflective mulch around plants. Reflective surfaces repel whiteflies.

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV) causes mottled light and dark green patterns on leaves, leaf distortion, and sometimes yellowing. It is extremely stable and can spread through contaminated seed, tools, and even by touch.

methods.instructions: Dip hands and tools in a solution of 1 part skim milk to 4 parts water before handling each plant. Milk proteins inactivate the virus.
